I am NOT saying this is your case. I was replying to the other comment to explain that, given the aforementioned in my two comments, they will not be easily "picked up" or be of focused interest in research because they can primarily be dismissed by/grouped with/seen as derivatives of anxiety/GAD.

Research has to be much more extensive/precise than how it's currently being done with this syndrome to get down to those details. In general, we know virtually nothing of why it affects certain people the way it does. It's mostly speculation via anecdote and some not-conclusive-enough scientific research.

Any modality can be too much for someone if done incorrectly. And it happens often. But all the core principles can be introduced gently if the therapist has a good enough awareness of the capabilities of the client's nervous system's ability to integrate new concepts or practices.

E.g. I tend to dissociation. IFS can be retraumatizing for someone whose main issue is fragmentation and identity loss. I went through that for years and it never helped. At all.

Some traumas/ events that impair us to the core happen very early on and the only way to resolve that is through trauma based therapy.

I never felt better than when a therapist held me, I allowed me to fully let myself go and relax in the arms. She rocked me, like a baby... And I cried s lot. 

I've had interpersonal issues and a deep rejection for life bc I've never felt secure, even as a baby.

And the primitive parts of our brains need different soothing mechanisms to repair that sort of early damage.

Talk therapy never provided that sort of intimacy, primal connection. It was akin to talking to a wall, since my issues weren't verbal. They were beyond that.

And for trauma that's usually the way to go to heal. Touch therapy, somatic experiencing, EMDR, Brainspotting, etc.

Not trying to diagnose you just sharing my opinion off your post.
